source: Car damage model (2026-10-16; owner on PR #33: 'pushing far in excess of safe values should ruin a part quicker; getting oil up to 170 C within 3 minutes should not be possible because the engine breaks first', and 'an engine without a real working cooling solution should keep running, but then other parts will start failing and that might cause the engine to shut off'). Every number here is [AS] (chosen for play, not measured on a real engine). Each part has one health-to-function translation (effect, factor = scale_at_zero + (1 - scale_at_zero) x health): the cooling parts cost radiator conductance or fan air, the engine internals raise the engine's friction (more heat into the oil, less power) and seize below seize_below, which shuts the engine off until the car is repaired. Each rule wears its part at a rate read off its curve over the excess past the safe value ([excess K, health lost per second], linear between points and on along the last segment beyond the table): a few kelvin past the safe value cost a part over many minutes, far past it ruins the part in seconds. The coolant rules count from the car's own overheat warning (cooling_system warnings.overheat_c, 118 C for the class defaults and the hypercar), the oil rules from absolute oil temperatures: 135 C is the setup check's oil limit (data/cooling_systems/cooling_upgrades.json oil_limit_c: an engine oil keeps its film to about 130-140 C), so a car the setup check passes never wears its internals; the stock hypercar's full-throttle run settles at 110.8 C oil on a 35 C day. Rules apply in file order every simulation tick; a dwell timer resets as soon as its signal drops below the safe value. The calibration against the owner's 2 MW / 11 bar hypercar run is in docs/damage_model.md (tests/unit/test_damage_engine.cpp [.][damage][long]).

parts.label: Radiator
parts.description: Boiled coolant scale and burst tubes: the radiator passes less heat to the air.
parts.source: [AS] a ruined core keeps a quarter of its heat-exchanger conductance (some tubes still flow).

parts.label: Radiator fan
parts.description: A cooked fan motor turns slower: less air through the radiator when the car is slow.
parts.source: [AS] a dead fan moves no air; ram air still flows at speed.

parts.label: Head gasket
parts.description: Combustion gas leaks into the coolant and forms pockets in the radiator: the cooling gets worse.
parts.source: [AS] gas pockets cost up to 40 % of the radiator's conductance.

parts.label: Crank bearings
parts.description: Thin hot oil lets the crank bearings rub: more friction, more heat in the oil, less power; worn through, they seize the engine.
parts.source: [AS] a scored bearing set triples the engine's friction before it locks up (physics_sim World::set_engine_wear scales the oil-viscosity friction of the engine plant); it seizes with 20 % of its life left (by then the friction it adds stalls a part-throttle engine anyway).

parts.label: Pistons and rings
parts.description: Scuffed pistons and rings drag on the bores: more friction and heat; worn through, a piston seizes in its bore.
parts.source: [AS] scuffed skirts and rings double the friction; a piston seizes with 20 % of its life left.

rules.source: [AS] 4 K past the overheat warning for 15 s: the coolant boils locally in the core; 10 K over costs about 4.5 % in 10 s, 30 K over 2 % a second.
[AS] the fan running flat out in overheated air for more than 30 s: about 5 % a minute, faster the hotter the air it pulls.
[AS] 12 K past the overheat warning (130 C for the class cars) the head warps against the gasket within seconds.

[AS] above 135 C the oil film thins: three minutes at 140 C cost 9 %, at 145 C a third of the bearings; at 155 C 1.5 % a second, at 165 C 10 % a second and at 170 C the film is gone (100 % a second). Calibrated on the owner's report (oil 190 C within 3 minutes): an oil temperature rising at 0.44 K/s seizes the bearings at about 161 C, 1 K/s at 166 C, 3 K/s at 169 C, before any worn-bearing friction is counted (test_damage_engine.cpp, the oil ramp case); a ramp faster than that is not one the engine thermal model produces.
[AS] above 145 C oil the piston skirts lose their oil film and scuff against the bores: 0.4 % a second at 155 C, 3 % at 165 C, 60 % at 170 C.
